A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe the same research, with matching authors, central mechanisms, experiments and Table 1. Their main text, figures, equations and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original CIFAR-10 classification and synthetic student-teacher regression simulations, including alignment, validation performance and training dynamics.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds experiments on model scale, sparsity, frozen parameters, input noise and neuron-level dynamics.

M1.justification: Appendix C.4 adds a formal extension from uniform decay γW to non-uniform decay γDW, with a corresponding quadratic regularizer. This changes the generalized update rule, but no experiment implementing this extension is reported. The original SGD/noise and RandomNN constructions remain unchanged.

E1.justification: CIFAR-10 classification and synthetic regression remain the dataset and task coverage. V2 Figure 14 adds regression with noisy inputs, extending input conditions beyond v1's parameter-noise experiments without introducing a new dataset or task domain.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains SGD, Adam, DFA and RandomNN for both model families. The normalized Hebbian and Oja comparisons, including pre- and post-activation variants, move from v1 Figure 4 to v2 Figure 18 unchanged. The alternative regularizers were also already evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: V2 adds evaluation designs using 1M, 10M and 50M parameter MLPs, CNNs, ResNet-18/34/50, sparsity and freezing fractions up to 95%, and input perturbations. These substantially broaden experimental settings and controls. The original SCE/SRE sample sizes and default learning rate, batch size and training duration remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds sensitivity studies of model scale, sparsity and frozen parameters, plus input-noise robustness tests. Figures 15, 19 and 20 provide additional evidence about learning-signal versus full-update dynamics, neuron-wise oscillations and their relationship to update magnitude, extending v1's analyses.

E5.justification: V1 already reports mean±SD with n=10 in Table 1 and temporal standard deviations in several plots. V2 explicitly identifies seeds, reports ten-seed means and standard deviations for Figure 3, and clarifies which retained figures depict single runs. These are reporting improvements, not evidence that previously stated run counts increased.

E6.justification: Table 1's numerical values remain identical, but Figure 3 contains revised estimates with newly specified ten-seed aggregation. Substantial added results show alignment in larger models, stronger alignment with sparsity, reduced alignment with freezing, and anti-Hebbian alignment under input noise with depth-dependent boundaries. These are additional findings, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Beyond v1's stationarity and noise derivations, Appendices C.4–C.5 add non-uniform-decay analysis, explicit assumptions, three lemmas, two near-stationarity theorems and a duration argument. However, the added Lemma 3 proof reverses the norm-integral inequality, and the revised continuous-time Equation 3 misorders the matrix product.

C1.justification: The central weight-decay/Hebbian and noise/anti-Hebbian claims remain. V2 emphasizes alignment before convergence and includes input noise in its abstract. It removes generalization deterioration from the introduction's contribution list and drops the Discussion's practical generalization-diagnostic claim, while retaining the corresponding empirical observations.

C2.justification: V2 adds a biological interpretation separating fast neuronal learning signals from slower biochemical weight decay and explicitly qualifies uniform decay's biological realism. It also distinguishes alignment of averaged directions for arbitrary rules from the stronger statistical alignment result for SGD, materially clarifying what the theory establishes.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies Gaussian sampling for synthetic data, the meaning of initialization multipliers, the width calculation for target model sizes, and the CNN architecture. The original SCE/SRE recipes, RandomNN implementation, hardware and stated compute time are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands its treatment of classical Hebbian feature learning, STDP, inhibitory plasticity and sparse coding, adding works including Sanger (1989), Clopath et al. (2010) and Brito and Gerstner (2016). It positions the proposed emergent mechanism as compatible with these functional accounts and develops the biological context beyond v1's algorithm-equivalence comparisons.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites the abstract, revises the introduction and discussion, subdivides related work, and systematically distinguishes learning signals from full weight updates. Expanded explanations, reorganized appendices and the new LLM-usage disclosure substantially change the narrative and document structure.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figures 9–12, 14–15 and 19–20, redraws Figure 3 with uncertainty bars and expanded layer labels, and moves v1 Figure 4 into the appendix as Figure 18. Retained figures receive expanded captions and are resized within a substantially different page layout; their underlying graphics otherwise remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: Broader controlled experiments, clearer uncertainty reporting and more careful interpretation strengthen the evidence for v1's central mechanism. However, the added formal material introduces errors, notably Equation 3's matrix ordering and the reversed inequality in Appendix C.5's Lemma 3 proof. The empirical and explanatory gains support a net improvement, but these mathematical defects limit the overall gain.
